model.label: Tax-funded national health service, run by 19 regions and two autonomous provinces within a national benefits package (LEA)

overview.statement: Article 32 of Italy's Constitution protects health as a fundamental right of the individual and an interest of society, and commits the Republic to free care for people who are indigent.

The National Health Service (SSN) covers every citizen and every foreign national who is ordinarily resident, and coverage is automatic; undocumented migrants are entitled only to urgent and essential care.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services? Coverage

overview.statement: The SSN is a universal, publicly financed service run by 19 regions and two autonomous provinces; the Ministry of Health sets priorities, passes tax revenue to them as block grants, and checks their performance through the New Guarantee System, which monitors delivery of the national benefits package (LEA).

Regional governments plan and deliver care through local health authorities (ASLs), which hold budgets and provide preventive, primary and hospital care; GPs and paediatricians are gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care, and the mix of public and accredited private hospitals differs widely between regions.
Italy set up its national health service (SSN) in 1978, replacing a fragmented social insurance system with a universal, tax-funded service modelled on the UK's NHS.

locator.section: Coverage and Access: Background and History

overview.statement: A 2001 constitutional reform moved more of the financing and delivery of care to the regions, while the national government kept responsibility for the Essential Levels of Care (LEA), the national benefits package.

locator.section: Coverage and Access: Background and History

financing.statement: The first regional tax that funds the SSN is IRAP, an earmarked tax on companies' value added (operating revenues minus costs) and on public-sector salaries; the review gives its standard level as 3.9%, which regions may raise by up to 0.92 points depending on the industry.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: The second regional tax is a regional surcharge on national personal income tax (addizionale IRPEF), which each region sets differently: some use a flat rate, others rates that rise with income.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: Each region's own revenue from these two taxes, plus expected patient co-payments, is compared with its assessed financial need; the national government covers the gap from an equalisation fund financed by national VAT.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: The five special-statute regions (Valle d'Aosta, Trentino-Alto Adige, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Sicily and Sardinia) receive a direct share of national tax revenue and are expected to fund the national benefits package from their own resources.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: National taxes do most of the equalising, but regional taxation is uneven: richer northern regions have larger tax bases and can add to the funding the central government sets, while the poorest southern regions have little room to raise extra money for health care.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: According to the Finance Ministry's 2025 monitoring report, the money set aside for the SSN comes from regional taxes (IRAP and the regional income-tax surcharge), the state's share of VAT, the tax shares of the special-statute regions and autonomous provinces, and a fixed amount of the regional services' own revenue.

locator.section: Capitolo 1 (Sezione I), financing of the SSN

financing.statement: The Finance Ministry's 2025 monitoring report states the fixed own revenue of the regional health services counted in SSN funding as just under EUR 2 billion, coming from patient co-payments (tickets) and doctors' private practice inside public hospitals (intramoenia).
Ordinary funding for the SSN was EUR 134.0 billion in 2024, equal to 6.1% of GDP, up from EUR 128.9 billion (6.0% of GDP) in 2023.

locator.table: Tab. 1.1: ordinary SSN financing, current health spending (national accounts) and GDP, 2015-2024 (EUR million); columns are years 2015-2024

financing.statement: Public sources paid for just over 73% of Italy's health spending in 2023, below the EU average of 80%; almost 90% of the remaining 27% was paid directly out of pocket.
In 2023, private sources accounted for nearly 27% of Italy's health spending, seven points above the EU average: out-of-pocket payments made up 24% and voluntary health insurance a further 3%.

Employer-run health funds, which mostly play a supplementary role, covered over 16 million people (27% of the population) in 2023, up from 7 million in 2013, largely because of tax incentives; WHO notes these estimates are uncertain.
The average annual contribution to a health fund was EUR 279 per person in 2021, and health funds held EUR 3.2 billion in resources in 2023.

The government encourages health funds through open enrolment, community-rated premiums and a tax incentive that lets employees deduct contributions to non-profit funds from taxable income; to qualify, a fund must be on the national register and spend at least 30% on services the SSN does not cover.

Commercial voluntary health insurance premiums totalled EUR 4.2 billion in 2023, up from under EUR 3.1 billion in 2019; around EUR 1.2 billion of the 2023 total was sold directly to individuals and the rest through health funds buying cover for their members.

Out-of-pocket health spending can be deducted from personal income tax at up to 19% after a EUR 129.11 threshold per taxpayer; for 2023, the Parliamentary Budget Office estimates the resulting tax refund at about EUR 4.6 billion, against EUR 43.1 billion of private health spending recorded by the Tessera Sanitaria system and EUR 26 billion declared by 22.8 million taxpayers.

In tax year 2023, about EUR 3.2 billion of contributions to health funds and mutuals qualified for tax relief, EUR 3 billion of it paid to bodies with an exclusively assistance purpose (type-B funds); the Parliamentary Budget Office estimates the lost personal income tax at about EUR 1.1 billion, over EUR 1 billion of it from type-B funds.

covered.statement: The SSN guarantees the national benefits package (LEA) throughout the country; regions may offer services beyond it only if they pay for them, and the services included are defined through positive and negative lists.

locator.section: How much is spent on health services? Coverage

covered.statement: Publicly covered services include preventive care, inpatient and outpatient care, maternity and primary care, medicines, mental health care, palliative care, rehabilitation, home visits and assistive devices.

locator.section: The Role of Public Health Insurance

covered.statement: The main coverage gaps are dental and mental health care: dental care is covered only for some groups, such as children under 14, and excludes orthodontic prostheses, while psychotherapy for people whose conditions are not severe, and smoking cessation, are generally unavailable.

locator.section: Box 2 What are the key gaps in coverage?

covered.statement: In 2023, public financing paid for 96% of hospital spending in Italy, above the EU average of 91%, and public coverage of retail medicines was slightly above the EU average.

Only 58% of spending on outpatient medical services was publicly financed in 2023, against an EU average of 77%; the 2025 profile links this partly to long waits for specialist visits that push patients to pay for faster private care.

The national benefits package was comprehensively revised in 2017, adding new vaccines, outpatient and diagnostic services, neonatal care and health devices, and a list of rare diseases covered by the SSN.

Italy has no dedicated long-term care insurance; instead a cash allowance (indennita di accompagnamento) is paid to people with severe functional limitations regardless of income, EUR 525 a month in 2022.
In 1978 Italy became the first country in Europe to close its mental hospitals, about 100 at the time, and to abolish compulsory treatment of psychiatric patients.

cost_sharing.statement: Primary care and inpatient care are free at the point of use for everyone; services that do carry charges have exemption categories (for example by age or income), but there is no overall annual cap on co-payments.

For outpatient specialist visits, diagnostic tests and dental care, each region sets a fixed co-payment (the 'ticket') per visit or test, ranging from a few cents to about EUR 36; for some specialties one co-payment covers up to eight interventions in the same area.
Patients who go to a specialist without a GP referral pay the full price out of pocket.

Twelve of the 21 regional health services charge fixed co-payments on outpatient prescription medicines, from EUR 2-4 per item to EUR 5-10 per prescription, with exemptions for some groups; the other nine charge none.
Every region applies reference pricing to reimbursable (class A) medicines, which WHO calls a source of 'avoidable co-payments'; the reference price must be at least 20% below the originator's price.

For outpatient specialist visits, income-based exemptions in all regions cover children under 6 and people over 65 in households with gross income under EUR 36,152, and unemployed people and pensioners over 60 in low-income households (under EUR 8,263 for a single person, up to EUR 12,910 with three or more children).

locator.table: Table 3. User charges for publicly financed health care, 2025: outpatient specialist visits, exemptions

cost_sharing.statement: Emergency department visits judged appropriate at triage are free, as is emergency transport; visits judged inappropriate cost EUR 25 plus a variable fixed charge for the care given (from under EUR 1 to EUR 36).

locator.table: Table 3. User charges for publicly financed health care, 2025: emergency care

cost_sharing.statement: Formal co-payments within the SSN are a small part of out-of-pocket spending: in 2023 the 'ticket' on specialist care and medicines made up only 7.4% of it (EUR 1.71 billion for specialist services and EUR 1.48 billion for medicines), and exemptions covered about 28% of specialist outpatient services delivered.
The 'superticket', a fixed EUR 10 surcharge on most outpatient consultations and diagnostic tests, was abolished in 2020, and the role of formal cost sharing has changed little since.

Out-of-pocket spending on retail medicines was EUR 10.6 billion in 2023, nearly 28% of pharmaceutical spending; it included about EUR 7.1 billion for non-reimbursed class C medicines and EUR 1.1 billion paid by patients who chose an originator over a reimbursed generic, a cost that was higher per person in the South (EUR 23.5) than in the North (EUR 13.3).

financial_hardship.statement: The 2024 health system summary says the SSN cannot always protect people from financial hardship, and that long waiting times are one reason people spend their savings or go into debt to pay for private care.

A 2017 estimate by RBM-CENSIS, cited in the 2022 review, put at nearly 8 million the number of people who, because of excessive waiting times, used all their savings on private care or borrowed to pay for health care, and at 1.8 million those pushed below the poverty line by health expenses.

Catastrophic health spending is heavily concentrated among low-income households: in 2022 it affected 27% of households in the poorest consumption quintile, and it was also above average in households headed by economically inactive, unemployed or retired people, older people living alone, households in the South and those with two or more children.
According to WHO, outpatient medicines and outpatient care are the main causes of catastrophic spending among poorer households, while for richer households dental care is the main cause.
Households in the lowest income quintile accounted for 60% of all catastrophic health spending in Italy in 2022.

additional_care.statement: Voluntary health insurance plays a minor, mainly supplementary role (faster treatment and more choice of provider), with a smaller complementary role covering co-payments and excluded services; it made up 2% of current health spending in 2023 and is sold by non-profit health funds and commercial insurers.
Health fund benefits are generally modest: some specialist outpatient care, diagnostic imaging and preventive dental care, with medicines rarely covered.
Under 'intramoenia', hospital doctors see patients privately outside their normal working hours, using the hospital's outpatient and diagnostic facilities, and the patient pays them.

Covered inpatient care has no user charges; extra billing for better accommodation applied to 0.5% of hospital admissions in 2019 and for choosing one's physician to 0.3%, with amounts varying by region and provider.

locator.table: Table 3. User charges for publicly financed health care, 2025: inpatient care

additional_care.statement: Registered health funds, which receive tax relief, grew from 267 to 324 between 2010 and 2023 and their members from 5.8 to 16.3 million between 2013 and 2023; in the latest year they paid out over EUR 3 billion, almost two thirds of it for services that substitute for, rather than add to, those the SSN guarantees.

access.statement: In 2023, 7.6% of Italians said they had gone without medical care because of long waiting lists, cost or access difficulties; waiting lists were the most common reason, affecting 2.7 million people, nearly twice the 1.5 million of 2019.
The waits are concentrated at the entry to specialist care: first consultations and diagnostic tests accounted for over 60% of waiting-related access barriers.

Once on a surgical list, Italian patients waited an average of 74 days in 2022 for a set of elective operations including cataract removal and hip and knee replacement, among the shortest waits in the EU; but this figure counts only the time from listing to surgery, not the often long wait for the consultations and tests needed before listing.

Initial data for the first half of 2025 showed urgent services (due within three days) delivered effectively, but less urgent care, over 75% of demand, lagging: for deferrable cardiology consultations with a 30-day target, only 75% of lists were cleared, after an average of 90 days.

locator.section: Box 1. Italy's new National Plan for Waiting List Management

access.statement: In 2024, 3.8% of Italian adults who needed medical care reported going without it because of cost, distance or waiting times, close to the EU average of 3.6%; but people at risk of poverty were 2.6 times as likely to report unmet need as the general population, against an EU ratio of 1.6.

In 2023 Italy had 5.4 doctors per 1,000 people, more than 25% above the EU average, but 6.9 practising nurses per 1,000, over 20% below the EU average of 8.4, giving one of the EU's lowest nurse-to-doctor ratios (1.3).

Over the past decade GP density fell by about 13% while overall physician density grew; in 2023 nearly 52% of GPs had more than 1,500 patients, the contractual maximum, and the national GP shortfall was estimated at 2,910 to 5,897 (8% to 16%), depending on the benchmark used.
Disparities are pronounced, particularly in the North: Lombardy alone would need a 20% larger GP workforce to meet contractual thresholds.

In 2023 over 8% of acute hospital admissions took place outside the patient's home region, rising to 21% in Calabria, 29% in Basilicata and 32% in Molise; this cross-region care cost nearly EUR 3 billion across 668,145 admissions, 84% of it going to northern regions.

In the 2023 New Guarantee System assessment, 13 regions met or exceeded the minimum standard in all three areas and 8 fell short in at least one; shortfalls were concentrated in prevention and community-based care and disproportionately affected smaller southern regions.

Italy had three hospital beds per 1,000 people in 2023, 40% below the EU average, and a hospital discharge rate 36% lower than the EU's, which the 2025 profile attributes to a long-standing strategy of reducing avoidable admissions.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy in Italy reached a record 84.1 years in 2024, the highest in the EU together with Sweden and six months above its pre-pandemic level.
Italy had the EU's second-lowest preventable mortality rate in 2022, with deaths from preventable causes about a third below the EU average.

Italy's age-standardised rate of deaths treatable through timely and effective care was about 30% below the EU average in 2022, mainly because of much lower mortality from ischaemic heart disease and colorectal and breast cancer.
The 2025 profile finds that Italy is very good at preventing avoidable deaths and has the lowest hospital admission rates for chronic conditions in the EU.
In the GBD 2019 study, Italy's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 89.6 (95% uncertainty interval 87.7-90.8) in 2019, 16.9 points higher than in 1990.

outcomes.statement: By age group in the GBD 2019 study, Italy's 2019 HAQ Index score was 92.2 for ages 0-14, 91.0 for ages 15-64 and 79.5 for ages 65-74.

locator.table: Table: HAQ Index estimates by location; row values in order: 2019 overall (0-74 years), young (0-14), working (15-64), post-working (65-74), then absolute change 1990-2019 for the same four groups

outcomes.statement: Cancer screening coverage remains below 2019 levels: breast screening of women aged 50-69 was 55% in 2023 against about 61% in 2019, and colorectal screening 35% against 40%.
The 2024 summary reports that 30-day mortality after hospital admission for a heart attack in Italy is among the lowest in Europe.

costs.statement: Italy spent 8.4% of GDP on health in 2023, 1.6 points below the EU average; per person spending was EUR 3,086 (adjusted for purchasing power), about 19% below the EU average, with public spending per person 27% below and private spending 8% above the EU average.
Real public health spending per person grew only 0.7% a year in 2015-2019 (EU average 2.9%), rose more than 9% in 2019-2021, then fell 3.5% in 2022 and 4.5% in 2023, back to its 2019 level.

Health's share of total government spending fell to a record low of 12% in 2023, which the 2025 profile attributes to fast growth in other spending, chiefly building-renovation tax credits and interest on public debt.
Long-term care takes only about 10% of Italy's health spending, against about 18% across the EU; roughly half of public long-term care funding is paid as cash benefits.

Hospital purchases of medicines overshot their ceiling of 8.15% of the National Health Fund by over EUR 3 billion in 2023, and by over EUR 4 billion in 2024 even after the ceiling was raised to 8.5%; under the payback mechanism, manufacturers and regions jointly cover the overrun.

In a study of 62 medicines with managed entry agreements over a three-year period, manufacturers paid back EUR 327.5 million, 0.9% of the EUR 41.1 billion public health facilities spent on medicines; financial-based agreements returned the most (EUR 158.1 million), outcome-based ones EUR 74.5 million and mixed ones EUR 94.9 million.

Regions that overspend must adopt recovery plans, which have typically meant cutting hospital beds, freezing staffing and outsourcing more to private providers; the Commonwealth Fund profile says these plans helped eliminate the SSN's overall deficit between 2007 and 2019.

what_works.statement: The 2024 health system summary judges the SSN generally efficient: with health spending well below the EU average, it provides access to high-quality treatment at a reasonably low cost, though with large differences between regions.

The 2025 profile says Italy's primary care system is strong and that this shows especially in diabetes management: although diabetes is more common in Italy than in most peer countries, Italy has the EU's lowest diabetes-related hospital admission rate.

Medicines the European Commission approved in 2020-2023 took on average 439 days to reach patients in Italy, against 578 days across the EU, and Italy reimbursed 83% of them, a share exceeded only by Germany (EFPIA WAIT survey 2024).

locator.section: 6 Spotlight on pharmaceuticals: access to new medicines

what_works.statement: Central procurement and strict governance have raised biosimilar use to about 67% of the addressable market by volume, against an EU average of about 32%.

locator.section: 6 Spotlight on pharmaceuticals: generics and biosimilars

what_works.statement: Italy has expanded medical training: medical graduates reached 16.6 per 100,000 people in 2023, 9% above the EU average, and over 50,000 residency contracts were funded in 2020-2024, nearly closing the gap between graduates and specialty training places.

Under payment-by-result agreements, AIFA tracks each patient's outcome against agreed clinical endpoints and the manufacturer refunds the cost if the treatment fails; these agreements yielded EUR 218 million in refunds and discounts in 2023, 72% from financial-based ones.

locator.section: Box 3. Italy is a European leader in the use of Managed Entry Agreements

what_works.statement: WHO notes as strengths of Italy's coverage policy that it is simpler than in many EU countries, that entitlement rests on residence (with refugees, asylum seekers and undocumented migrant children entitled to all benefits), and that no region uses percentage co-payments.

problems.statement: WHO finds co-payments widely applied with no exemption for most working-age people on low incomes and no cap on co-payments.
WHO finds that the 19% tax rebate on out-of-pocket health spending above EUR 129 a year favours people with higher incomes.

Nursing graduate numbers have fallen steadily since their 2013 peak, to a record low of 16.3 per 100,000 people in 2022, less than half the EU average; applicants per nursing place fell from 1.6 in 2019 to 1.04 in 2024.
In 2024 a quarter of medical residency posts went unfilled, including 30% in emergency medicine and 15% in clinical pathology.

The Commonwealth Fund profile, citing the 2022 system review, says regions under recovery plans, mainly in the South, have had longer waits, less investment and reduced access to services, and that studies show worse health outcomes there.

In 2024 seven regions (Abruzzo, Calabria, Campania, Lazio, Molise, Puglia and Sicily) were under financial recovery plans, and two of them, Calabria and Molise, were also run by a nationally appointed health commissioner, a step taken when a region keeps failing on both finances and essential services.

Generics made up only 29% of pharmaceutical volume in 2024, against over 50% in the EU, and in 2023 patients paid an estimated EUR 1.06 billion in avoidable out-of-pocket costs to get branded medicines when generics were available.

locator.section: 6 Spotlight on pharmaceuticals: generics and biosimilars

problems.statement: Antibiotic consumption reached 23.1 defined daily doses per 1,000 people a day in 2023, 16% above the EU average, and the ECDC's antimicrobial resistance index ranks Italy sixth-worst in the EU.
WHO reports that the procedures and deadlines for updating the benefits package (LEA) are set in law but rarely followed, so the package is not regularly updated.

locator.table: Table 4. Gaps in publicly financed and VHI coverage: service coverage

problems.statement: Screening shows a north-south gap: in 2022 fewer than 12% of eligible women in Calabria took part in organised breast cancer screening, against nearly 50% in several northern regions.

Unmet need for dental care is unequal: in 2024, 12.5% of people at risk of poverty who needed dental care went without it because of cost, distance or waiting times, against 4.6% of the general population.

reforms.statement: Italy's new waiting-list plan makes 'patient protection pathways' legally binding: if the guaranteed deadline cannot be met, the local health authority has to offer the patient another timely option, either a different public or accredited provider or a private service paid for with public money; national funding is EUR 50 million for 2025 and EUR 100 million a year from 2026.

locator.section: Box 1. Italy's new National Plan for Waiting List Management

reforms.statement: The plan's centrepiece, a national waiting-list monitoring platform, began operating in July 2025.

locator.section: Box 1. Italy's new National Plan for Waiting List Management

reforms.statement: In July 2025 the government opened talks on a consolidated pharmaceutical law (Testo Unico) that would modernise the payback mechanism so that it becomes a contingency tool used only when preventive controls fail.
A 2025 reform made 'innovative' status for medicines a stricter yes-or-no rating, dropping the 'conditionally innovative' category; the status is now granted per indication for at most 36 months.

From the 2025 academic year, the multiple-choice entrance exam for medicine was replaced by an open first semester (semestre filtro), with progression decided by a national test at its end; the authorities also plan to train 30,000 more physicians by 2032 than under unchanged policy.

locator.section: Box 2. An ambitious plan to scale up medical education

reforms.statement: In 2024 Italy changed how pharmacies are paid, from percentage margins on retail prices, which rewarded dispensing pricier medicines, to a fixed fee per pack plus a lower percentage margin, to encourage generic use.

The National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) allocates EUR 16 billion to health in 2021-2026, over 8% of Italy's plan, for infrastructure and digital systems, community care through telemedicine and the health workforce.

With PNRR money, the electronic health record (FSE 2.0) covered 98% of the population and almost all GPs were connected by 2024, but digital readiness still differs markedly between regions because of the SSN's decentralised governance.
Decree 77/2022 set new models and standards to strengthen primary and community care in line with the PNRR, covering community care networks and facilities and telemedicine.

locator.section: Box 4 Are efforts to improve integration of care working?

reforms.statement: The 'psychologist bonus', introduced in December 2021 to help people with anxiety, stress, depression and psychological fragility linked to the pandemic and the economic crisis, was made a permanent part of the benefits package by the 2023 Budget Law, with EUR 5 million for 2023 and EUR 8 million a year from 2024 for psychotherapy sessions.

us_lessons.statement: In a 2025 paper comparing US and Italian systems of care for severe brain injury, the authors judged the biggest difference to be access linked to funding: Italy's public system guarantees care across the whole continuum, while US private insurance is complex and hard to navigate.

The same authors write that, apart from military and work-related injuries, most people with severe brain injury in the US face major barriers to uninterrupted care, and that the resulting gaps add to the very high societal cost of brain injury in the US.

The comparison found the US ahead on home and community-based services for brain injury, which in Italy are mostly delivered through longer inpatient stays or day-hospital programmes, while Italy gives more priority to involving family caregivers in rehabilitation.

In the US, the authors identify funding as the main factor deciding whether a person with acquired brain injury gets rehabilitation, with the very wealthy and those already on Medicare or Medicaid facing the fewest barriers.
